# The research question

Psychology relies on samples, and how much you trust a finding depends partly on
who was in the study. When a paper doesn't report the demographic makeup of its
participants, you can't judge how far the claim reaches, and a later meta-analysis
can't tell who the literature speaks for. This is the sample representativeness
question, and it has two dimensions: a descriptive one and a temporal one.

I address both. First, how often do psychology papers report participant
demographics (gender, race, education, socioeconomic status)? Second, has that rate
changed from 2010 to 2026, and does it differ across subfields or across the
COVID-19 disruption?

I restrict this to a single venue, PLOS ONE, for tractability. It's high-volume,
multidisciplinary, and fully open access, so I can retrieve the whole corpus and
read it by machine instead of hitting paywalls. That's what makes a study across
tens of thousands of articles feasible instead of a hand-coded sample of a few
hundred.

Since hand-coding doesn't scale to that volume, I delegate the reading to a large
language model. For each qualifying paper, the model reads the methods text and
returns the reported demographics in a fixed structured format, which I then
aggregate into reporting-rate trends.

## Temporal design

To track change over time I split the window into four periods that reflect
distinct eras:

| Stage | Years | Rationale |
|-------|-------|-----------|
| Early | 2010 to 2014 | Baseline era |
| Middle | 2015 to 2019 | Settled, pre-pandemic |
| COVID | 2020 to 2023 | Pandemic disruption |
| Post-COVID | 2024 to 2026 | Recovery |

# The extraction schema

For every distinct participant sample a paper describes, I code whether each
demographic was reported and in how much detail:

| Demographic | Coded fields |
|-------------|--------------|
| Gender | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (male / female / other) |
| Race | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (white / black / hispanic / asian / other) |
| Education | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage with versus without college |
| Socioeconomic status | An ordinal 0/1/2 code: 0 = not reported, 1 = reported only categorically (e.g. "low income"), 2 = reported with a numeric threshold (e.g. below $30,000) |

Two things about the schema are deliberate and they matter.

The unit is the participant sample, not the paper. One paper can report several
independent samples, and I code each as its own row, tied together by the shared
article ID (its DOI). Collapsing a paper's samples into one row would discard real
within-paper variation and bias the reporting-rate estimates.

Each row also carries article-level metadata: publication date, the corresponding
author's institution, and the full PLOS subject taxonomy for the paper. These
support subgroup analysis and let me track where each row came from.

## Inclusion criteria

A paper enters the corpus only if it's an empirical research article (not an
editorial, correction, or review), published in PLOS ONE, filed by PLOS under
psychology (any subfield), and dated between 2010 and 2026. I set no minimum sample
size.

# Pipeline architecture

The system is a straight line of stages, each one producing something the next
stage consumes:

```
1. Enumerate qualifying psychology articles  ->  master index (58,467 articles)  [DONE]
2. Draw a stratified pilot sample            ->  46 articles                      [DONE]
3. Run the model over the pilot              ->  extracted demographics            [NEXT]
4. Adjudicate pilot accuracy by hand         ->  proceed / revise decision
5. Run the model over the full index         ->  full demographics table
6. Aggregate the table                       ->  reporting-rate trends (the result)
```

Stages 1 and 2 are done and verified. The rest of this document covers how I built
them and what the later stages still leave open.

## Computing environment

The pipeline runs on Rivanna, UVA's high-performance computing cluster. Two
constraints drive that. The model is too large for commodity hardware and needs
several high-memory GPUs at once. And the full extraction over 58,467 articles is
embarrassingly parallel, so I split it across many workers to finish in reasonable
wall-clock time. The orchestration is written to survive preemption and lost
sessions, since individual jobs run for hours.

# Decision 1: data acquisition

This was the most consequential design choice, and the reasoning is worth recording
in full, because I only reached the final setup after my first approach ran into
the realities of the corpus. I started with one plan, hit four separate problems,
and ended up with a different, more defensible design.

## The initial approach: bulk local corpus

PLOS distributes an open dataset, allofplos, with every PLOS article as a JATS XML
file. I ingested the whole thing: roughly 391,000 articles, about 9 GB compressed,
held on the cluster. Each file embeds not just the article text but PLOS's nested
subject taxonomy, encoded as tags:

```
Biology and life sciences  ->  Psychology  ->  Social psychology
```

The appeal was self-containment: parse the taxonomy from each file, keep the
psychology articles, and never depend on a network service again. My parser
descended to the subfield one level under a "Psychology" node:

```python
def get_psychology_subfields(article):
    """Return the psychology subfield(s) an article is tagged with.
    e.g. Biology > Psychology > Social psychology  ->  ["Social psychology"]
    """
    subfields = []
    for node in article.subject_nodes:
        if node.text == "Psychology":
            # grab the tag(s) nested one level under Psychology
            subfields.extend(child.text for child in node.children)
    return subfields
```

## Problem A: taxonomy schema drift

My first version returned zero psychology articles. I diagnosed it by dumping the
raw taxonomy block from a few recent articles and reading it directly. The tags
were there, but the container around them had been renamed. PLOS labels each
taxonomy block with a type attribute; older articles use "Discipline", newer ones
use "Discipline-v3". My parser matched the exact string "Discipline", so it
silently excluded every modern article.

The fix was to match any type that starts with "Discipline", which covers both. The
broader lesson, which recurred, is that PLOS's encoding hasn't stayed constant
across fifteen years of publishing, so I validate structural assumptions against
the corpus rather than a single example.

## Problem B: subfield vocabulary mismatch

The original plan named five target subfields: social, cognitive, developmental,
clinical, and quantitative psychology. Checking against the corpus surfaced two
mismatches. PLOS's controlled vocabulary has no "Quantitative psychology" term at
all, so that one would have matched nothing. And PLOS uses several subfields the
plan didn't list, including Experimental psychology, Psychometrics, Behavior, and
Emotions.

Rather than force a preset list the taxonomy doesn't honor, I chose to include all
subfields. The design became taxonomy-driven: I keep every article PLOS files under
Psychology and record whatever subfield PLOS assigned, regardless of the original
five. This stays faithful to how the field organizes itself and lets me aggregate
or subset by subfield later. In the finished corpus that's 23 subfields, not five:

Addiction, Applied psychology, Behavior, Cognitive psychology, Collective human
behavior, Developmental psychology, Emotions, Experimental psychology, Gender
identity, Instinct, Neuropsychology, Pain psychology, Personality, Psychological
adjustment, Psychological attitudes, Psychological defense mechanisms,
Psychological stress, Psychology (unspecified), Psychometrics, Psychophysics,
Relaxation (psychology), Sexual identity, and Social psychology.

The breadth is worth noting. Some are standard subfields (social, cognitive,
developmental psychology), some are broad topic areas PLOS files under Psychology
(Behavior, Emotions), and a few are narrow or barely about human participants
(Instinct, plus animal-behavior work PLOS still tags under Psychology). Whether to
analyze all 23 or narrow to a defined core is one of the open questions at the end.

## Problem C: the 2015 discontinuity

With the taxonomy parsing correctly, I ran the full scan over all 391,000 files and
built a first master index. A routine integrity check, counting psychology articles
per year, exposed a gap that no plausible mechanism could explain as signal:

```
2014: 2,002 articles
2015:    12 articles    <- implausible
2016: 2,100 articles
```

A near-empty year between two full ones points to a defect, not a trend, so I
investigated rather than proceeding.

My first hypothesis was date parsing: perhaps 2015 articles were being misdated and
pushed into adjacent years. I ruled it out by building a year histogram over all
PLOS ONE articles regardless of subject, which showed 2015 fully populated with
correctly dated articles. The articles existed and were dated correctly; they
simply weren't being recognized as psychology.

My second hypothesis pinned the failure on subject detection in 2015. I set up a
per-year comparison between how many articles my parser tagged as psychology and
how many merely contained the substring "psych" in their raw tags (the counts below
are the values I observed at the time):

```
year | total articles | tagged psychology | contains "psych"
2014 |      594       |        37         |         38
2015 |      561       |         1         |          1
2016 |      435       |        35         |         35
```

That was decisive. For 2015, even a naive substring search returned almost nothing,
which meant those articles had no subject taxonomy at all, not taxonomy in an
unexpected shape. Dumping the raw taxonomy block from several 2015 articles and
tallying the type attributes across the year confirmed it: almost every 2015
article contained only

```xml
<article-categories>
  <subj-group subj-group-type="heading">
    <subject>Research Article</subject>
  </subj-group>
</article-categories>
```

a bare document-class heading and no subject taxonomy at all. The count was clear:
of 561 sampled 2015 articles, 557 had no subject tags in their distributed files,
as did about 37% of 2013 articles.

This is a property of the data PLOS distributes, not a defect in my code. PLOS
classified these articles in its own systems but, for that interval, never wrote the
taxonomy into the downloadable files. A label that was never written can't be read.
Left uncorrected, this would have voided most of 2015 and a substantial part of
2013, invalidating the Middle stage and any trend line crossing that interval.

## The resolution: Solr for discovery

The taxonomy is absent from the distributed files but not from PLOS itself. PLOS
runs a Solr search index that holds the authoritative subject classification for
every article, including the ones whose files omit it. So I inverted the
architecture: use the search index to determine which articles qualify (discovery),
and keep the local files only for the full text the model has to read. That split,
search index for discovery and local corpus for full text, is what the original
plan proposed before I attempted the bulk-local shortcut.

## Problem D: query construction

Getting the discovery query right took two more corrections, each isolated by
adding one constraint at a time and watching the result count.

First, the index holds far more than whole articles; it also indexes fragments like
sections and figures. Without a specific `doc_type:full` filter, the query returns
several million of those fragments instead of articles. Second, the constraints
have to be issued as strict filter queries. A loosely written query is interpreted
permissively by the endpoint and returns essentially the whole date range instead
of just the psychology subset.

With both corrections applied, each constraint narrows the count coherently:

```
q=*:* only                  : 3,487,529   (all indexed units, incl. fragments)
+ doc_type:full             :   411,419   (whole articles, all journals)
+ journal:"PLOS ONE"        :   332,150
+ article_type Research     :   313,425
+ date = 2015               :    28,107   (PLOS ONE research articles, 2015)
+ subject Psychology        :     4,346   (2015 psychology, recovered)
```

The operative query is a conjunction of filters:

```python
filters = [
    'doc_type:full',                       # essential: whole articles only
    'journal:"PLOS ONE"',
    'article_type:"Research Article"',
    'subject:"Psychology"',
    f'publication_date:[{year}-01-01T00:00:00Z TO {year}-12-31T23:59:59Z]',
]
```

Under the search-index approach, 2015 recovered from 12 articles to 4,346. The
index returns each subject as a full path, for example /Biology and life
sciences/Psychology/Cognitive psychology/Language, and I read the subfield as the
segment immediately after "Psychology", which preserves the meaning of the earlier
XML parser.

## Operational issues of note

Two cluster-specific failures also came up, both the kind that quietly consume time
when they aren't documented.

Batch jobs kept failing with a missing-dependency error even though the software was
installed. The cause: the usual command for activating the software environment
behaves differently inside a non-interactive batch job than in an interactive
shell; it appeared to succeed but left the job bound to the wrong interpreter. I
fixed it by invoking the correct interpreter by absolute path and skipping
activation.

Separately, a long-running preprocessing step launched in a terminal background was
killed whenever the connection dropped, because the web terminal tears down its
process group at session end. I now submit that work as a scheduled job, which runs
independently of any terminal. Both fixes are encoded in the run scripts.

## Data-quality handling

The pipeline tolerates two defects I saw in the corpus. One article file was
truncated and wouldn't parse; the scanner logs it and skips it rather than aborting
a multi-hour job over one bad file out of 391,000. And about 6% of the articles the
search index returns, mostly recent 2025 and 2026 papers, aren't in the local file
snapshot, so there's no retrievable full text; I flag those and exclude them from
sampling so the pipeline never tries to code an article it can't read.

# The finished master index

Under the search-index approach the per-year counts are continuous, with no
residual gap:

```python
total: 58,467 psychology articles
by year:
  2010:  853   2014: 4,249   2018: 3,492   2022: 3,761
  2011: 1,886  2015: 4,346   2019: 3,219   2023: 3,761
  2012: 2,481  2016: 3,663   2020: 3,548   2024: 4,249
  2013: 4,478  2017: 3,367   2021: 3,714   2025: 5,009
                                            2026: 2,391 (partial year)
by stage:
  early: 13,947   middle: 18,087   covid: 14,784   post-covid: 11,649
```

The lower 2010 count reflects PLOS ONE's smaller early publication volume, a real
feature of the venue rather than an artifact. The 2026 count is partial because the
year is incomplete.

# Decision 2: the pilot sample

Before committing to a full run, I test the model on a small batch and check the
output by hand. Two properties of the sampling design matter.

The sample is stratified, not simple random. A simple random draw would be
dominated by high-volume subfields like social and cognitive psychology and might
omit the rarer ones entirely, but the point of the pilot is to test the model
across the full range of writing conventions. So I draw two articles from each
subfield in the index.

The draw is reproducible. It's seeded with a fixed value, so I can regenerate the
identical sample, which is a basic requirement for a transparent, auditable
process.

```python
def stratified_sample(articles, per_subfield=2, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)                     # fixed seed = reproducible
    picked = []
    for subfield in all_subfields(articles):      # every subfield present
        candidates = [a for a in articles if subfield in a.subfields]
        if len(candidates) >= per_subfield:       # skip subfields with too few
            picked += rng.sample(candidates, per_subfield)
    return picked
```

The realized sample is 46 articles across the 23 subfields listed earlier.

# Decision 3: model selection

The original plan offered two candidate models, of which I was to select one:

| | Mistral-7B | Llama-3.3-70B (selected) |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | 7 billion parameters | 70 billion parameters |
| Structured-extraction accuracy | Lower; more prone to omission and fabrication | Higher; more reliable |
| Compute cost | Modest; runs on limited hardware | Substantial; requires multiple high-end GPUs |

I selected Llama-3.3-70B. Accuracy is the binding criterion, because a missed or
fabricated demographic value feeds straight into the reporting-rate estimates that
are the study's output. Running on Rivanna removes the compute-cost consideration
that would otherwise favor the smaller model. The pilot exists precisely to test
whether that choice holds up before the full run.

# Extraction mechanics

I submit each article's text to the model with an instruction that fixes both the
extraction targets and the output format:

```text
You are coding a psychology research article for a systematic review of
demographic reporting. For EACH distinct participant sample, code the four
demographics defined by the schema above (gender, race, education,
socioeconomic status), and for each one, whether it was reported and, where
reported, its breakdown.

Respond with ONLY a JSON array, one element per sample, with these exact keys...
```

Two safeguards keep the output honest. It's schema-validated, so a response must be
well-formed structured data with exactly the required fields; anything malformed is
rejected and flagged rather than quietly admitted to the dataset. And I move the
methods and participants sections to the front of the submitted text, since that's
where demographics are reported, which concentrates the relevant signal near the
start of the prompt for long articles.

# Scaling the full run

Running 58,467 articles through a 70-billion-parameter model is compute-intensive.
I split the work into independent shards that run concurrently across many GPUs.
Each shard writes its own output file, and the run is safe to restart: an
interrupted shard skips the articles it already finished and resumes, which is
essential for multi-hour jobs subject to preemption.

# Aggregation and inference

Given the completed demographics table, the final stage computes two quantities for
each demographic, for each year, and separately for each of the four stages. The
reporting rate is the share of samples that report a given demographic. The mean
composition is, for example, the average percentage female among samples that
reported gender. Tracking these from 2010 to 2026 is the study's answer: whether
demographic reporting in psychology is improving, and how the trajectory differs
across the early, middle, COVID, and post-COVID periods.

# Reproducibility

All the code and documentation is version-controlled on GitHub
(SJ-Jain-systems/Halle). Each stage is its own testable module:

```
src/
  solr_client.py          discovery via the PLOS Solr search index
  build_index_solr.py     materialize the master index of 58,467 articles
  jats_xml.py             parse metadata and full text from the article files
  sample_articles.py      draw the stratified pilot sample
  extract_demographics.py the model instruction and schema validation
  model_backend.py        model execution on the GPUs (vLLM / transformers)
  run_pipeline.py         full run, sharded and restartable
  analyze_trends.py       reporting-rate aggregation by year and stage
docs/
  DECISIONS.md            the three decisions, with full reasoning
  RUNNING_ON_RIVANNA.md   step-by-step run instructions for the cluster
  SCORING_RUBRIC.md       the pilot adjudication rubric
scripts/                  the diagnostics that isolated the 2015 gap and more
tests/                    33 automated tests over the non-model logic
```

Two points are worth emphasizing for anyone auditing this. The non-model logic is
covered by 33 automated tests spanning parsing, filtering, sampling, and
aggregation; the model itself is validated by hand-coding the pilot. And the
diagnostic scripts that isolated the schema drift and the 2015 gap are kept in the
repo, so the evidence behind each design decision remains inspectable.

# Open questions

Three decisions would benefit from input before the full run.

1. Subfield scope. The taxonomy yields 23 psychology subfields, some broad
   (Behavior, Emotions) and some barely about human participants (for example
   animal-behavior work filed under Psychology, or Instinct). Do I analyze all 23,
   or narrow to a defined core of human-participant subfields, and if so which?

2. Coverage at the boundaries. Pre-2011 articles use the older tagging generation,
   and some 2025 to 2026 articles lack local full text. Are the earliest and latest
   years complete enough for a fair longitudinal comparison, or should I bound the
   window (for example 2011 to 2024)?

3. Validation threshold. What level of pilot accuracy, measured against the scoring
   rubric, justifies proceeding to the full run, and who does the hand-coding?
